Summit

/SUM-it/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Summit is highest level that can be reached.

Climbers finally reached the summit after nearly ten hours.

Worked Example

After twenty years of tournaments, a chess grandmaster finally wins the world championship. There is no higher title left in the game — every rank she ever aimed for now sits below her.

She has reached the single highest point her field offers, with nothing above it — that ultimate peak is the summit. Summit is more precise than 'top' because it names the absolute highest point that can be reached, not just a high position.

How Summit Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

peak

peak: the pointed top of a mountain

Antonyms

base

base: the lowest, supporting part of something

nadir

nadir: the very lowest point possible

How Strong Is It? — hilltop → crest → peak → summit

hilltop vs. summit

hilltop vs. summit: A hilltop is lower-key than a summit — a hilltop is simply the top of a small hill, while a summit is the very highest point that can be reached.

crest vs. summit

crest vs. summit: Crest is weaker than summit; the crest is the top ridge of a hill or wave, but the summit is the single highest point of all.

peak vs. summit

peak vs. summit: Peak is slightly weaker than summit — a mountain range has many peaks, but each mountain's one absolute highest point is its summit.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — summus

Root — summus: highest (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Summit traces to a single Latin word: summus, 'highest.' The summit is the highest point - and the same root gives us sum, because Romans added columns of numbers upward and wrote the total at the top. There is no prefix or suffix to peel off; the whole word stands at the top on its own.

Use the root in a new word: summary

Use the root in a new word: summary: Her summary captured the chapter's main points in one paragraph.

Root Check

Word Choice

Summit works literally for a mountain's highest point (reach the summit) and figuratively for a high-level meeting between leaders (a climate summit) — both senses point to reaching the highest point, whether physical or diplomatic.
